conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Maya Bennett—I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician, which simply means I specialize in the emotional well-being of new mothers like you.  

I’d like to spend a few quiet minutes with you using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—most people just call it the EPDS. It’s a short set of questions that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, so we can be sure you’re getting the support you deserve.  

Everything you share stays completely confidential within our care team, and there are no right or wrong answers—only what’s true for you. We’ll go through ten questions about the past seven days; each one is an invitation to check in with yourself, and we can pause or revisit anything that feels hard.  

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:  

Over the past week, have you still been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

Honestly, most of the time I can still laugh—like yesterday my partner made a goofy face while changing the baby’s diaper and I burst out giggling. But it’s not quite as easy or frequent as before I gave birth. I have to be in the right mood, and sometimes I feel too tired or preoccupied to find things funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, like I said, I can still laugh—just not as often or as freely as before. Sometimes it takes a little more effort, or I have to be in a better moment, but it hasn’t disappeared completely.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do still look forward to some things—like my mom coming over to help or the little walk I take with the stroller most afternoons—but the excitement isn’t as strong as it used to be. It feels more like “that’ll be nice” rather than a real spark.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… that happens. Last night the baby was extra fussy and I kept thinking maybe I’m not feeding him right or I missed some cue. I told myself I “should” know better, even though my partner kept saying it’s normal. I catch myself doing that a few times a week—feeling like little problems are somehow my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little bit, yeah. Like, I’ll suddenly wonder if the baby’s breathing when he’s napping, even though the monitor looks fine, or worry that a tiny rash means something awful. I can usually calm myself down pretty quickly, but those random anxious flashes pop up most days.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky—more like a quick wave of “what if something bad happens?” that passes in a minute or two. I haven’t had any full-blown scares, just those little surges of worry that fade once I check on the baby or distract myself.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. Like this morning—he wouldn’t settle after the 3 a.m. feed, laundry was piled up, and I felt I couldn’t get one clear minute to even brush my teeth. For a moment it felt like everything was sliding out of control. I usually pull it back together, but that “snowed-under” feeling hits me a few times a week.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, it’s not that bad. I do get sad once in a while, but it hasn’t really messed with my sleep—maybe just a night or two when I couldn’t drift off right away because my mind was busy. Once I drop off, I stay asleep.
I have felt sad or miserable
Yeah… I do feel sad or kind of flat a few days a week. It usually comes and goes—like I’ll tear up while feeding him for no clear reason—but it’s not an all-day, every-day thing.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

That’s happened—maybe once or twice this past week. It’s usually when I’m already tired and everything feels a little overwhelming, like when he wouldn’t latch and I just sat there crying for a few minutes. It passes pretty quickly, but the tears do come.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—nothing like that. I’ve felt tired or low, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

You've shared that, while you can still laugh and enjoy small moments, the spark isn't as bright as before: joy feels dulled and excitement is muted. Several times a week you blame yourself when the baby is fussy, worry that something awful might happen to him, and feel snowed-under by ordinary tasks. Sad or flat moods drift in a few days a week, and you've found yourself crying briefly when things pile up. Sleep is mostly intact and you've had no thoughts of harming yourself. You're working hard to care for your baby and stay afloat, and it sounds exhausting.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 14, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient still anticipates events but describes markedly dulled excitement, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>The mom reports self-blame "a few times a week," fitting "some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive worries about baby's safety that arise without cause and occur "most days," aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent episodes of feeling overwhelmed several times a week, indicating intermittent difficulty coping, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>"A few days a week" and tearing up without cause map semantically to "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 14 meets the threshold for probable major <med>depression</med> with peripartum onset. <sym>Anhedonia</sym> (<quote>isn't as strong as it used to be</quote>) plus <sym>low mood</sym> several days a week align with DSM-5 Criterion A. Multiple cognitive/affective symptoms (self-blame, worry, tearfulness) support clinical concern. Score on Q10 is 0, so immediate safety risk is absent, yet functional load is high. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med>
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med> and discuss medication options compatible with breastfeeding
3. Arrange practical support-partner/family to handle a night feed, meals, or household tasks-to improve rest and reduce overload
4. Start daily mood tracking and brief self-care routines (shower, 10-minute outdoor walk, balanced snacks) to monitor patterns and stabilize energy
5. Keep crisis numbers handy: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline and your local emergency department for any safety concerns
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient: 0–6 mo post-delivery, self-report

Symptoms endorsed  
- Anhedonia: reduced ability to laugh/feel excitement (Q1, Q2)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame several times per week (Q3)  
- Mood lability: tearfulness 1–2×/week, “flat” mood several days/week (Q8, Q9)  
- Sub-threshold anxiety: daily unprompted worries about infant safety, brief surges of “what-if” fear (Q4, Q5)  
- Feeling overwhelmed / “snowed-under” multiple days/week, usually resolves with support (Q6)  

Associated factors  
Sleep: Night-time sleep generally preserved; occasional brief initial insomnia (Q7)  
Safety: Denies self-harm thoughts (Q10)  
Function: Maintains basic self-care and infant care with support

Pattern  
Mild, intermittent depressive and anxiety symptoms present ≥2 weeks; no current safety concerns; functioning partially preserved with external help.

Screening significance  
Meets partial criteria for minor/ subsyndromal postpartum depression and comorbid anxiety; does not meet threshold for major depressive episode. Recommend formal clinical interview (PHQ-9, GAD-7, EPDS) and psychosocial support evaluation.
